say.text: A leg with varicose veins. You raise the leg to empty the veins, press firmly over the saphenofemoral junction, and ask the patient to stand.
With the pressure still on, the veins fill again from below. Which structure is letting blood in?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The junction is squeezed, so blood cannot arrive from above. Where else could blood reach the superficial veins?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the junction is the spot you pressed, so it looks like the leak.
But the pressure sits on the junction, so it blocks reflux from the junction itself. Filling that continues under the pressure must enter somewhere else.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The junction is the pressed site, but the question asks what keeps refilling while the pressure is on, which is a different question.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the deep veins are what the tourniquet tests examine, so deep disease feels like the cause.
But this pattern is a junction-and-perforator test. Deep obstruction shows up on walking with a tourniquet, not on standing with the junction pressed.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Deep obstruction is a walking test, so keep it separate from a standing test with the junction pressed.

say.text: Yes. Pressing the junction stops reflux from above, so filling that continues under the pressure must come through an incompetent perforator.
Worked case, every step shown. Step 1: raise the leg so the veins empty. Step 2: press over the saphenofemoral junction. Step 3: the patient stands, and you watch the veins.
Step 4: release the junction. Rapid filling from above means junctional incompetence. Filling that stays while the pressure is on points to the perforators. This is the Brodie–Trendelenburg test.
Second patient, same steps: the veins empty, the junction is pressed, and the patient stands. Nothing refills while the pressure is still on.
You release the junction, and the veins refill rapidly from above. Which structure is incompetent?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Only the junction was pressed. Ask where the blood came from once that pressure was released.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because perforators are the vessels that do fill the superficial veins, so they feel like the answer to any filling.
But that filling pattern belongs to the moment the pressure is still on. Here nothing refilled under the pressure, so look at the pattern after release.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Match the pattern to the moment: filling under pressure belongs to one structure, filling after release to the other.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the deep veins are what the walking tests examine, so a refill problem feels deep.
But this refill pattern is the junction test. Deep obstruction is read with a tourniquet and walking, not with the junction pressed.
Yes. Nothing refilled under the pressure, so the blood was blocked at the junction. Rapid refilling from above on release points to junctional incompetence.
A 46-year-old with varicose veins. A tourniquet goes on the thigh and she walks. Her calf aches, and the bulging veins do not empty.
Which test was done, and what does the result mean?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Walking with a tourniquet on tests the deep system. Blocked deep veins cannot empty on walking. Which name goes with the walking test?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the two test names are easy to swap, and the junction is the site you already know them for.
But the junction test compresses the junction and watches the veins on standing. This patient was walked with a tourniquet on, which is a different maneuver.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The two names are easy to swap, so match each name to its own maneuver before you trust it.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the test name is right, and the result feels like it belongs to the junction.
But a walking test with a tourniquet reads the deep veins, so the junction is the wrong thing to name here. Look at what the pain and bulging say.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The name is right; the error lies in the meaning you attached to it.

say.text: Perthes: tourniquet on, the patient walks. Veins empty if the deep veins are open and the perforators competent. Calf pain and bulging veins mean the deep veins are blocked.
Brodie–Trendelenburg is the other test: compress the junction, stand, and watch. Rapid refilling from above means junctional incompetence.
Yes. Pain and bulging on walking with the tourniquet on mean the deep veins are blocked, which is what the Perthes test reads.
You want the surgery that flush-ties the great saphenous vein at the junction, through a groin incision.
Which Trendelenburg is it?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the Brodie–Trendelenburg name is the one you use most at the bedside, so it sticks to every Trendelenburg.
But that name is a bedside test for junctional reflux. Read the noun that follows the name, because it says what is done.

sure_note.text: You were sure the bedside name fits the surgery. A test and an operation are different things, so check the noun first.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because a sign is something you find on examination, so the word feels like a finding about the vein.
But the Trendelenburg sign is hip abductor weakness, a finding in the standing leg that has nothing to do with the vein.

choices.label: Show me the four side by side

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the posture is used when you set up the bedside test, so it feels like part of the procedure.
But the Trendelenburg position is a body posture, not a vein procedure.

choices.label: Show me the four side by side

say.text: Four names, one word each. Brodie–Trendelenburg: a bedside test for junctional reflux. Trendelenburg sign: hip abductor weakness.
Trendelenburg position: a body posture. Trendelenburg operation: flush ligation of the great saphenous at the junction.
Yes. The Trendelenburg operation is flush ligation of the great saphenous at the junction, with its tributaries tied as well.
A patient is listed for varicose vein treatment. You need the one test that is the investigation of choice.
Which test do you order?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test shows the reflux, the perforators and the deep veins together, not just one of them.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a bedside Doppler finds junctional reflux quickly, so it feels like the whole investigation.
But it is a screening step that stops at the junction. It does not map the whole limb.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A bedside Doppler is a screen; the question asks for the full map, so check what the test reports.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because venography is the classic picture of the deep veins, so it feels like the gold standard for everything.
But venography is reserved for complex deep disease or planned deep intervention, not the routine work-up for varicose veins.
Think of a ladder. Hand-held Doppler detects junctional reflux at the bedside, and stops there.
Colour duplex maps the reflux, the perforators and deep patency in one scan. Venography is for planned deep intervention.

choices.label: Go on to the next question

say.text: Yes. Colour duplex is the investigation of choice, because one scan shows reflux anatomy, perforators and deep patency.
Before you plan junctional surgery, the junction, the perforators and the deep veins all need examining. You want one test that covers all three.
Which one?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Count what the test must show: three structures at once. Which single examination can show all three?
That choice is not right. It is tempting because a clinical test answers the junction question quickly, so the picture feels covered.
But a clinical test for junctional incompetence says nothing about the perforators or the deep veins.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because the deep veins are the hard part of the work-up, and venography shows them in detail.
But detail on the deep system is reserved for complex deep disease, and it is not the routine map before superficial surgery.
Yes. Colour duplex maps the junction, the perforators and the deep veins in one examination.
Your registrar wants the great saphenous stripped this afternoon. The junction refluxes on the scan.
What must be confirmed before you operate?

choices.label: Confirmed junctional reflux is enough to operate
Deep vein patency, on Perthes or duplex
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where the blood will go once the superficial veins are removed, and whether the deep system can take it.
That choice is not right. It is tempting because reflux on the scan is the indication for surgery, so it feels like permission to operate.
But reflux shows that the superficial veins are incompetent. It does not show where their blood will go once they are removed.

sure_note.text: You were sure reflux was enough. Reflux tells you what is leaking, not whether the deep system can take the flow.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is tempting because the junction test decides where to operate, so a positive result feels like the go-ahead.
But a positive junction test says what is refluxing. It does not say whether the deep veins are open to take the flow.
Superficial vein surgery removes the route the blood uses. If the deep veins are blocked, the superficial veins become the collateral outflow.
A positive Perthes test, meaning deep obstruction, is a contraindication to stripping or ligation. Confirm deep patency first, by Perthes or duplex.
Yes. Deep vein patency comes first, because blocked deep veins make the superficial veins the collateral outflow.
